items.value: India's energy decision-making is increasingly complex and interconnected — the passage lists many interlinked problems and promising trends together
items.reasoning: The passage never delivers a single verdict; it stacks up interlocking strands — fossil fuel supply, energy access, imports, pricing and governance, land/water/air contestation, efficiency programmes, urbanisation and transport policy, renewables — and closes by saying 'all is not bleak'. That structure is itself the message: the decisions are many-sided and entangled. (C) is wrong because the passage explicitly refuses the bleak reading; (D) is contradicted by the demand-side items (energy efficiency, transport policy); (B) is unsupported — sustainable development goals are never mentioned, let alone said to drive policy.

items.value: Antibiotics should be used only therapeutically, not as growth promoters in livestock
items.reasoning: Every element of the passage targets non-therapeutic use: antibiotics 'fed to poultry and other livestock as growth promoters', companies stopping the drugs used 'to make chickens gain weight faster', and Denmark banning 'antibiotic growth promoters' — after which it produces more pigs that 'get fewer diseases'. (C) overshoots: it is growth promotion that Denmark banned, not treatment, and the passage's own evidence is that animals stayed healthier. (A) and (B) recommend abandoning animal-source food, which the passage never suggests — indeed it reports pork output rising.

items.value: Neither assumption is valid — the passage blames high fuel prices without naming oil-producing countries, and locates no food crisis geographically
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 substitutes an actor for a price: the passage lists 'high fuel prices' among the blamed factors but never says who or what makes them high, so 'oil producing countries are one of the reasons' is imported from outside the text. Assumption 2 shifts the crisis's location: the passage says mass consumption in emerging economies 'could be well poised to create a food crisis' — the crisis is caused by demand there, but nothing says the crisis itself will occur there rather than worldwide. Runner-up: (B), 2 only. It would win if 'create a food crisis' is read as a crisis inside those same countries; I set it aside because the passage's frame is world food prices, so the crisis it fears is a global one.

items.value: Neither assumption is valid — the passage calls GDP growth important, not essential to developed status, and guarantees no distribution of income
items.reasoning: Assumption 2 fails on its own words: the passage hedges with 'In theory' and says households, communities and governments become 'increasingly able to set aside some funds' — an enabling tendency, not a guarantee, and it says nothing about income reaching all households. Assumption 1 makes a necessity claim ('essential') and invokes a category ('developed country') the passage never uses; describing income growth as development economics' 'central message' asserts its importance, not its indispensability. Runner-up: (A), 1 only. It would win if 'the importance of income growth' is read as presupposing that a country cannot become developed without rising GDP; I set it aside because the passage's closing note on GDP's outsized place in the 'development lexicon' reads as description of a convention rather than endorsement of a necessity.

items.value: Q and T
items.reasoning: Apply the three filters in turn. Gazetteers are the books that are not law reports: since P, R and S are law reports, the Gazetteers are Q, T, U and V. Old means not new: S and U are new, so among the Gazetteers the old ones are Q, T and V. Blue covers belong to R, Q and T only, so V (red) drops out and Q and T remain.

items.value: The wrong term is the second term 2; it should be 0
items.reasoning: Split the series by position. The odd-place terms are 3, 7, 13, 21, 31, 43, rising by 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. The even-place terms are 2, 4, 10, 18, 28, 40, rising by 2, 6, 8, 10, 12 — every gap matches the odd series except the first, which should be 4. Working back from 4 with a gap of 4 gives 0, so the 2 is the intruder. The correction is confirmed by a second relation: each even-place term is its odd-place partner minus 3 (7−3=4, 13−3=10, 21−3=18, 31−3=28, 43−3=40), and 3−3=0.

The letters form a Latin square — row 1 is B, A, C and row 2 is C, B, A, each using all three letters once, as does each column. Row 3 already has A and C, and the third column already has C and A, so the missing letter in both is B. The entry is 3B.

Sequence-I is generated by multiplying successively by 0·5, 1·5, 2·5, 3·5, 4·5: 8×0·5=4, 4×1·5=6, 6×2·5=15, 15×3·5=52·5, 52·5×4·5=236·25. Applying the same multipliers to the starting value 5 gives A=5×0·5=2·5, B=2·5×1·5=3·75 and C=3·75×2·5=9·375. Note that 2·5 and 32·8125 are also offered — they are the values of A and D respectively, so reading the wrong position, not the wrong rule, is the trap here.

items.value: Both are correct — they meet after exactly 5 hours, each having walked 7·5 km, i.e. midway
items.reasoning: Add the distances hour by hour. X contributes 1·5 km every hour; Y contributes 1, 1·25, 1·5, 1·75, 2 km. The gap closed after each hour is 2·5, 5·25, 8·25, 11·5, 15 km, so the 15 km is covered exactly at the end of the fifth hour — statement 1 holds. In those five hours X has walked 1·5×5 = 7·5 km and Y has walked 1+1·25+1·5+1·75+2 = 7·5 km, each exactly half of 15 km, so they meet midway — statement 2 holds too.

items.value: 3 papers were below 60% (they score 40%, 48% and 56%)
items.reasoning: Let the marks be 5k, 6k, 7k, 8k, 9k, 10k and the maximum per paper be M. The ratio sums to 45, so 45k = 60% of 6M = 3·6M, giving k = 0·08M. The six papers are then 0·40M, 0·48M, 0·56M, 0·64M, 0·72M and 0·80M — that is 40%, 48%, 56%, 64%, 72% and 80%. Exactly three of these fall below 60%.

items.value: Religious denominations tend to ignore the unity of man
items.reasoning: The argument runs from denominations to a conclusion about mankind as a single body: once each denomination judges the others, no religion can be right, so 'all the world is right or all the world is wrong'. The passage can only reach that verdict by treating humanity as one, which is precisely what denominational judging of one another disregards. The other three are absent from the text: nothing says a man must belong to a denomination (A), nothing imposes a duty to propagate (B), and nothing claims men misunderstand their own faith (D).

items.value: The best dominion is the one that pursues unity and frames laws that make good citizens
items.reasoning: The passage names the two failings that make a commonwealth bad — it 'has neither enough pursued the end of unity, nor framed its laws with sufficient forethought' — and adds that 'men are not born fit for citizenship, but must be made so'. Inverting those failings gives exactly (C). (A) is contradicted, since the passage's whole point is that disorder varies between commonwealths rather than being inevitable; (D) is the despairing opposite of a text that explains how a dominion succeeds; (B) overstates by making the sovereign solely responsible for 'all the problems', where the passage only says the fault lies less with subjects' wickedness than with the state of the dominion.

items.value: Assumptions 1 and 2 are valid; equality underpins confident participation and inequality damages democracy
items.reasoning: Assumption 3 is ruled out at once: the passage treats equal standing as a norm that inequality violates and calls equality a moral 'default principle' now part of commonsense morality — an ideal it takes to be realisable, not unattainable. That eliminates (B) and (D), leaving assumption 1 in either surviving option. Between 2 and 4, assumption 2 sits directly on the opening sentence, 'Inequality violates a basic democratic norm', so harm to democracy is exactly what the author takes for granted; assumption 4 recommends putting the right to equality into our values, which the passage says has already happened ('is by now part of commonsense morality'). Runner-up: (C), 1 and 4. It would win if 'violates a democratic norm' is judged too weak to support a claim about democracy's survival, while the passage's prescriptive turn ('persons should not be discriminated on grounds such as race, caste, gender...') is read as urging equality into our everyday political vocabulary.

items.value: Every form of government destroys itself through excess of its own defining principle
items.reasoning: The passage is built as three parallel cases: aristocracy 'ruins itself by limiting too narrowly' the circle of power, oligarchy by 'the incautious scramble for immediate wealth', and 'even democracy ruins itself by excess of democracy'. The repeated verb and the word 'even' mark the shared mechanism as the point. (C) inverts the role of education, which the passage cites only as the missing ingredient, and overclaims a 'perfect' democracy; (A) is a bland observation the passage never makes; (D) reads tyranny as inherent in all government, whereas the passage derives tyranny specifically from democracy pushed to excess.

items.value: 30 or more (the number lies between 30 and 70)
items.reasoning: The group holds 80 Indians and 120 − 80 = 40 foreigners, with 70 English speakers in all. The count of English-speaking Indians is smallest when as many foreigners as possible speak English: with all 40 doing so, 70 − 40 = 30 Indians remain. It is largest when all 70 English speakers are Indian, which is possible since 70 ≤ 80. So the figure can be anything from 30 to 70, and the only option covering that whole range is '30 or more'. (B) names only the minimum and (C) points the inequality the wrong way.

items.value: Both hold — S = 666m, which is 9 × 74m; for the digits 3, 6, 9 the sum is 3996 = 74×54 = 9×444
items.reasoning: Three distinct digits give six arrangements, and each digit occupies each place exactly twice, so S = 2(a+b+c)×111 = 222(a+b+c). Because the digit sum is a multiple of 3, write a+b+c = 3m, giving S = 666m. Since 666 = 9 × 74, S is always divisible by both 74 and 9. The reading in which the digits themselves are the non-zero multiples of 3 — that is, 3, 6 and 9 — gives the same verdict concretely: 369+396+639+693+936+963 = 3996 = 74 × 54 = 9 × 444.

items.value: Only statement 1 is certain; Class-B's average must fall, but Class-A's may rise or fall depending on who leaves
items.reasoning: Every score in Class-A is at most 21, while every score in Class-B is at least 22, so Class-B's average is at least 22. Adding four students who each score below that average necessarily pulls it down, whichever four move — statement 1 is certain. Statement 2 is not: Class-A's scores span 17 to 21, and the question never says which four leave. If the four lowest scorers go the average rises, but if the four highest go it falls, so no definite increase can be asserted.

items.value: Either statement alone fixes Seema at 6th from the top
items.reasoning: In a class of 40, a rank r from the bottom is 41 − r from the top. Statement-1: Priya is 31st from the bottom, so 10th from the top, and being 4 ranks below Seema puts Seema 4 places higher, at 6th from the top — sufficient on its own. Statement-2: Ena is 37th from the bottom, so 4th from the top, and Seema is 2 ranks below her, again 6th from the top — also sufficient on its own. Since each works alone and the two agree, (C) is correct and (D) is wrong because neither statement needs the other.

items.value: Statement-1 alone settles it — C is the heaviest
items.reasoning: Statement-1 places A and D above B, E and F, and then rules out A and D as the heaviest. That leaves nobody among A, B, D, E and F who can be heaviest, so the heaviest must be C — the answer follows from Statement-1 alone, even though it never names C. Statement-2 gives only C > A > D and says nothing about B or E, so it cannot on its own establish who tops the group; that makes (B), (C) and (D) wrong.
